title: HIPAA security and privacy rule
why: Health data in the United States carries obligations that are not derivable from the product's own rules: the medium, the minimum-necessary test, break-glass access, a six-year audit retention and a named business associate. The catalog's retention rule covers deletion of a record, not the legal basis for holding it or the evidence that access was legitimate.

addRequirements.title: PHI is encrypted at rest and in transit
addRequirements.statement: When protected health information is stored, transmitted or backed up, the application shall encrypt it in transit and at rest with a configured key that is rotatable without a rewrite.
addRequirements.definition: A {primary} record that contains PHI is unreadable without the key, on every path it travels, including backups and the export path.
addRequirements.failurePath: If the key is missing or rotation fails, the application refuses the operation rather than writing plaintext as a fallback.
acceptance: Given a stored PHI record, when the underlying storage is read directly, then no field of it is readable plaintext.
Given any request that logs or raises an error while handling PHI, when the log and the message are inspected, then neither contains a PHI value.
Given a backup and a restore, when the backup medium is examined, then it is encrypted with the same key policy as primary storage.

addRequirements.title: Access to PHI is limited to the minimum necessary
addRequirements.statement: When a {secondary} reads protected health information, the application shall return only the fields the caller's declared role and workflow require.
addRequirements.definition: A role that needs a name and an appointment time cannot read a diagnosis through the same endpoint, even though the database holds both.
addRequirements.failurePath: If the required-field set for a role is not declared, the request is refused rather than defaulting to every field.
acceptance: Given two roles with different declared field sets, when each reads the same record, then each response contains only its own fields.
Given a request that names extra fields, when it is processed, then the extra fields are dropped server-side rather than trusted.
Given a disclosure, when the access log is read, then it names the fields returned.

addRequirements.title: Emergency access is possible, exceptional and reviewed
addRequirements.statement: When a {secondary} needs access outside their normal permissions in an emergency, the application shall require an explicit break-glass action with a stated reason, grant it for a bounded time, and surface it to a reviewer within one day.
addRequirements.definition: The product can be used in an emergency without weakening the default path: the exception is logged, time-boxed and visible.
addRequirements.failurePath: If the review queue is unavailable, the break-glass grant still expires on time; an unreviewed exception is never equivalent to an approved one.
acceptance: Given a normal user, when they attempt a break-glass read, then they must supply a reason and the grant is time-boxed.
Given an expired break-glass grant, when the same user retries, then access is refused without a new reason.
Given a break-glass event, when the review report runs, then the event appears with actor, reason, target and duration.

addRequirements.title: Audit records are retained for six years and cannot be edited
addRequirements.statement: The application shall retain every access and change record for protected health information for at least six years in storage that rejects update and delete.
addRequirements.definition: An audit entry written today is still readable, and still attributable, six years from now.
addRequirements.failurePath: If audit storage rejects a write, the operation it describes fails: an unaudited change to PHI is never allowed to succeed quietly.
acceptance: Given a PHI change, when the audit sink is unavailable, then the change is refused and the failure is reported.
Given an audit record, when the application is offered an update or delete, then the storage rejects it.
Given any PHI access older than the retention policy allows to expire, when retention is evaluated, then the record is kept.

addRequirements.title: Every business associate is inventoried and contracted
addRequirements.statement: The application shall name every third party that can receive protected health information, record the agreement that permits it, and refuse to send PHI to a party with no recorded agreement.
addRequirements.definition: The list of parties who can see PHI is written down, current, and enforced by configuration rather than by memory.
addRequirements.failurePath: If a vendor is added to the configuration without a recorded agreement, the send is refused at runtime rather than discovered in an audit.
acceptance: Given a configured destination with no recorded agreement, when PHI would be sent to it, then the send is refused and logged.
Given the inventory, when a new integration is added, then the build fails until the agreement record is present.

addRequirements.title: A breach has a runbook with an owner and a clock
addRequirements.statement: The repository shall contain a breach-notification runbook that names an owner, the detection signals, the decision log and the notification deadlines that apply.
addRequirements.definition: A person discovering a suspected breach has a document that tells them who to call next and by when, and someone has already walked through it.
addRequirements.failurePath: A runbook naming no owner, no deadline or no decision record is treated as missing, not as present.
acceptance: Given the runbook, when a reviewer reads it, then it names an owner, the notification deadlines and where the decision log lives.
Given a drill, when it is executed, then it produces a timestamped record of each step and who performed it.

addGates.statement: A PHI field is unreadable in raw storage and in logs, proven by a test.
Audit records for PHI are append-only and the retention period is configured, proven by a test.
